conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you've been having trouble swallowing and keeping food down. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started about a week ago. I get this burning pain when I swallow—like a knife going down. It’s worse with solids, but even liquids hurt. I’ve only been able to keep toast down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve been vomiting after meals, but no blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. Vomiting almost every time I eat. No blood, though. And I don’t have belly pain—just tenderness if I press on my upper stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any fever, weight loss, or recent illness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I haven’t had a fever or lost weight. No sick contacts or new foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. We did a CT scan earlier, and it didn’t show anything like a blockage or pancreatitis. Your lipase was normal, so that’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had pancreatitis before, but this doesn’t feel the same. I’m just so nauseous all the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’re going to admit you so we can get you IV fluids and figure out what’s causing this. We’ll likely involve gastroenterology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I just want to be able to eat again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. The GI team reviewed your case. They’re recommending an endoscopy—EGD—tomorrow to look inside your esophagus and stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I’m a little nervous about it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s very safe. You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel anything. It helps us see if there’s inflammation, ulcers, or anything else causing your pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds okay. Will they take samples?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they may take small biopsies if they see anything unusual. We’ll talk about the results after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a hiatal hernia before—could that be it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. Hiatal hernias can contribute to reflux and pain. But we need to rule out other things like esophagitis or motility issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on omeprazole for years. Shouldn’t that help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should, but sometimes symptoms persist. We’ve switched you to IV omeprazole for now to make sure you’re getting full effect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you just got back from your endoscopy. The good news is your esophagus looks normal—no ulcers or severe inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right? So why does it hurt so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They did see some mild irritation at the junction of your esophagus and stomach, and some redness and erosion in the antrum—part of your stomach. That’s called antral gastritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Gastritis? Could that be causing the pain when I swallow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might contribute, but usually gastritis causes more upper belly discomfort. Still, we’ll treat it with the PPI and see if symptoms improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They took biopsies, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, from the junction and the antrum. Those results will take a few days. We’ll follow up with your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I did have one episode of diarrhea right after eating—food just came out undigested.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s important. We’re scheduling a barium swallow test tomorrow to see how food moves through your system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be moving too fast?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a possibility. Some people have rapid transit, especially after certain surgeries or with nerve issues. We’ll see what the test shows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, the barium test is back. Good news—your swallowing muscles are working fine, and there’s no blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a small hiatal hernia, which we already suspected. More importantly, the barium reached your colon in 10 minutes—much faster than normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I had that diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Food is moving through your small intestine too quickly. We call this rapid transit. It can cause cramping and diarrhea soon after eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there anything I can do about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Try eating smaller, more frequent meals. Increase fiber—like oats or psyllium. Avoid drinking liquids 30 minutes before and after meals. Lying down after eating might help slow things down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can try that. And my swallowing pain—is it gone for good?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been tolerating liquids and soft foods without pain, which is great. We think the combination of gastritis and the hiatal hernia was triggering it. The PPI should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds? I was worried about the iron and minocycline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Since the endoscopy didn’t show pill esophagitis, it’s safe to restart them. Just take them with plenty of water and stay upright after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. And the biopsies?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Those are still pending. You’ll need to follow up with your GI doctor to discuss the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re doing much better. We’ll send you home with your regular meds, including the PPI twice daily, and instructions on diet changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel like I can finally eat again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it slow with solid foods. And please keep that GI follow-up—we need to review the biopsy results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll talk to my PCP about my meds too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re cleared to go home. Rest, take care, and call if symptoms come back.
